r: This course teaches learners to build instructional design models, manage design projects, write assessments, and develop curriculum by applying a design-thinking process to real instructional problems. The applied deliverables — needs analyses, learning objectives, storyboards, and design documents — are exactly the artifact types generative tools already draft competently, and observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical work is the largest AI-usage category, with design and writing tasks classified by task-exposure research as positively associated with exposure. No licensure or accreditation body names this course, so the binding constraint is the design-exposure of the work itself rather than an institutional floor. At 24 months, AI drafts components of an instructional design plan competently but still requires a human to define strategy, sequence decisions, and manage stakeholder constraints, keeping the rating at Medium rather than High.

By 2031, AI systems will plausibly execute most of an instructional design cycle end to end — needs analysis, objective writing, curriculum mapping, and assessment alignment — since real-deliverable evaluations already show top models reaching roughly half of expert-level wins on comparable occupational deliverables, and capability continues to compound on a multi-month doubling trend. The design-thinking process this course teaches becomes something students increasingly direct an AI system through rather than perform by hand, eroding the instrumental need to practice the underlying steps manually. No licensure or accreditation mandate protects the course, and its foundational role is limited since only one later course in this cluster names it as a direct prerequisite. Verification burden remains moderate — a misaligned curriculum is correctable, not catastrophic — so the rating rises to High, with real uncertainty about how fast adoption inside instructional-design workplaces actually proceeds.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems performing the bulk of routine instructional-design production — drafting objectives, storyboarding, and aligning assessments — competently enough that the manual-execution rationale for this course is substantially eroded, even as firm-level adoption of AI overall remains uneven and macro productivity gains from AI have so far been modest rather than transformative. What plausibly endures is the design-thinking judgment behind the artifacts: framing an instructional problem, choosing among competing solutions, and evaluating whether an AI-produced design actually serves learners, none of which is locked in place by licensure or accreditation. The rating holds High under a wide-uncertainty band; if firms move slower than capability suggests, or if the discipline reorients the course toward directing and auditing AI-generated designs, some of that exposure could translate into a differently structured but still-necessary course rather than eliminate it entirely.
EDT 2050.d: This course serves as an introduction to instructional design theories and practices. It introduces different instructional design models, management, assessment, curriculum design & development, and instructional design pathways. Design thinking process is integrated throughout the course. It also includes intensive study of both practical instructional design processes and applications in order to solve real world instructional challenges.

r: The course pairs conceptual content — responsible digital citizenship, social media literacy, and how shifting instructional modalities change design strategy — with the applied production of a digital portfolio, resume, and interview practice. Portfolio and resume writing sit among the most AI-exposed tasks in the evidence base: professional-writing studies show large time savings and quality gains when AI assists drafting, and writing is one of the categories task-exposure research classifies as strongly positively associated with exposure. Interview practice retains a live, interpersonal component that resists full automation, but its preparation is increasingly AI-assisted too. No licensure or accreditation mandate touches this course, and it functions as a terminal application course rather than foundational scaffolding, so the binding constraint is simply how exposed its core deliverables already are. Rating Medium at 24 months, reflecting substantial but not yet complete erosion of the manual-production task.

By 2031, AI writing assistance will draft polished portfolios, resumes, and application materials essentially on demand, and productivity research already shows professional writing tasks completed dramatically faster with assisted drafting, at equal or higher rated quality — evidence directly applicable to this course's culminating artifacts. Digital-citizenship and social-media literacy content, largely conceptual and discussion-based, is similarly well within AI's explanatory range. The interview-practice component is the most resistant piece, since real-time interpersonal responsiveness sits outside the categories task-exposure research treats as automatable, but AI-based mock-interview coaching tools are already diffusing into career-services contexts and will likely be more common by this horizon. With no institutional lock-in and only a terminal role in the curriculum, the course's instrumental rationale shifts toward directing and evaluating AI-produced career materials rather than producing them unaided, pushing the rating to High.

A decade out, generating a competent portfolio, resume, and cover letter will be trivial for AI, and diffusion research suggests that even if only a modest share of firms have fully integrated such tools by the mid-2020s, adoption compounds further over ten years even as macro productivity effects remain gradual. The remaining human task is less about producing these artifacts and more about authentic self-representation and live interview performance, an embodied, real-time interpersonal skill that stays comparatively resistant. Digital-citizenship literacy also persists as a genuine need, since navigating an AI-saturated information and social environment responsibly is arguably more relevant, not less, at this horizon. With no licensure floor and a terminal curricular position, the rating remains High under real uncertainty about exactly how career-services practice reorganizes around AI tools, rather than about whether the manual-production rationale for the course continues to erode.
EDT 2060.d: Digital Life and Learning explores the vast landscape of instructional design issues and considerations that span beyond established development models and theories. This course empowers students through the study of responsible digital citizenship, social media, a deep understanding of how changing modalities affects design strategies, and the complexities of developing instruction in a digital landscape. The course culminates with real world application of gained knowledge and skills through the creation a digital portfolio, resume, and practicing interview skills.

r: Preservice teachers in this course research and develop technology-integrated classroom lessons, participate in projects modeling effective integration, and use technology for professional development — applied work that blends AI-exposed content production (lesson materials, research summaries) with classroom-facing pedagogical judgment about which tools actually serve K-12 learners. That judgment component, plus the course's role preparing teacher candidates within an educator-preparation curriculum whose content areas Colorado's licensure framework requires programs to address, functions as a binding constraint distinct from raw task automatability: it is not a specific clinical placement, but neither is it a freestanding elective a program could drop without restructuring. AI can already draft sample lessons integrating a given tool, yet at 24 months the instrumental need for teacher candidates to build this integration judgment themselves, inside an accredited program, is essentially unchanged. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI lesson-planning and tool-recommendation assistants will be common in K-12 settings, and the jagged-frontier evidence is instructive here: teachers who blindly accept AI-suggested technology integrations without understanding pedagogical fit risk measurably worse outcomes for students outside the tool's actual competence, which keeps a real verification role for the human. The course's content — selecting, managing, and evaluating technology in classrooms — increasingly becomes about supervising AI recommendations rather than researching integrations from scratch, a genuine erosion of the original task. But the educator-preparation curriculum this course sits within continues to require coverage of instructional-technology competency for licensure candidates, capping the rating rather than letting it collapse. The instrumental case shifts from producing integration plans to critically evaluating AI-generated ones, landing the rating at Medium as base automatability rises alongside persistent programmatic requirements.

A decade out, AI tools embedded directly in classroom platforms may handle much routine tool selection and lesson-technology matching, and the honest central case has instructional-technology practice looking substantially different from today's course content. But teacher-licensure programs in Colorado still need to demonstrate that candidates can integrate technology purposefully and equitably, and that programmatic requirement does not evaporate absent a change to the licensure framework itself — the sort of institutional shift that moves far more slowly than model capability. The deeper uncertainty is pedagogical: whether this becomes a course about auditing AI-generated integration plans for developmental and equity appropriateness, or is folded into a broader technology-and-teaching sequence. Either way, some version of the competence — judging whether a technology choice actually serves K-12 learners — remains instrumentally necessary, holding the rating at Medium rather than collapsing it to Low or releasing it to High.
EDT 2100.d: This course is designed to provide preservice teachers with skills and experiences that will allow them to effectively and appropriately integrate technology into teaching and learning activities. This course will focus on actively participating in projects that model effective technology integration, researching and developing classroom lessons and activities that utilize emerging technologies, and using technology to support professional development activities.

r: This course covers multi-platform networking concepts and terminology for K-12 and training settings, alongside copyright law, fair-use, Acceptable Use Policies, and accessibility issues in networked environments — a mix of technical vocabulary AI explains readily and compliance judgment with real consequences if applied wrong. Misconfigured network policy, a mishandled copyright claim, or an inaccessible learning platform each carries genuine institutional and legal exposure, so verification of AI-generated guidance in this domain still needs a human who understands the underlying rules, a materially protective factor here. Positioned after the department's fundamentals course and contributing to broader educator-technology competency expectations without being a specific board-mandated course itself, the institutional constraint here is only partial. AI-usage data shows technical and computing content among the most AI-engaged categories, but at 24 months the compliance-literacy core of this course is not meaningfully displaced. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will draft network-policy language, accessibility remediation plans, and copyright-compliance checklists fluently, and diffusion of such tools into IT and instructional-support functions will be further along, though unevenly across institutions. The jagged-frontier problem is sharp in this domain: an AI-suggested Acceptable Use Policy or accessibility fix that looks plausible but misses a jurisdiction-specific legal nuance is exactly the kind of non-obvious failure that raises verification burden rather than lowering it, keeping a knowledgeable human load-bearing. Educator-technology competency expectations continue to touch this content area, though not this exact course by name, which caps rather than removes the erosion. The instrumental case shifts from manually researching network and compliance concepts toward critically checking AI-generated policy and accessibility guidance for institutional and legal soundness, landing the rating at Medium as underlying task automatability rises but compliance verification still binds.

A decade out, network administration and compliance drafting will likely be heavily AI-mediated, and the specific technical vocabulary this course teaches may matter less than the judgment to catch where an automated recommendation is legally or ethically wrong for a given K-12 context. Verification burden is the factor most likely to hold up over ten years: accessibility law, copyright doctrine, and network-security practice all evolve, and an AI system trained on older norms can fail in ways that are not obvious to someone without the underlying literacy. Educator-technology expectations persist in the central case, contributing to but not single-handedly mandating this course. The wide uncertainty is over how thoroughly networking fundamentals get folded into broader instructional-technology coursework by 2036, not over whether some human capacity to evaluate AI-generated network and compliance guidance remains necessary. Rating holds Medium, protected chiefly by verification burden rather than by institutional lock-in.
EDT 2200.d: Students enrolled in this course will focus on the concepts and terminologies of multi-platform (MacOS and Windows) networked learning environments for the purpose of instruction in K- 12 educational and instructional training settings. Participants will learn networking concepts, terminology, vocabulary, and structures which will enable communication among teaching and technical professionals. Students will learn to apply critical thinking to situations and scenarios which hamper the implementation and utilization of networks in learning environments. Students will be exposed to copyright law and fair-use guidelines including the implementation and enforcement of Acceptable Use Policies (AUPs). This course will also explore legal and ethical usage of networks, including accessibility issues with adaptive software.

r: Prospective teachers here survey emerging educational technologies, select and evaluate tools for teaching, build multimedia projects and web-based learning environments, use interactive whiteboards, and address copyright, e-plagiarism, cyberbullying, and security issues, aiming to graduate as leaders who disseminate technology integration through personal learning networks. Multimedia production and tool-comparison content are AI-exposed, but selecting and evaluating a technology's fit for a specific K-12 classroom, and leading colleagues in adopting it responsibly, are judgment-and-presence tasks bound up with the licensure-adjacent educator-preparation curriculum this course sits inside — Colorado's framework for approving teacher-preparation programs expects technology-integration competency to be addressed, even though it does not name this exact course. That partial institutional tether, plus the leadership and in-person coaching dimension of the course, keeps the instrumental need essentially intact at 24 months despite AI's fluency with the underlying content. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will generate multimedia projects and web-based learning environments quickly and will suggest technology integrations for given lesson goals, and observed-usage data continues to show computer-and-writing tasks as the largest categories of actual deployment, meaning teacher candidates will encounter these tools constantly in practice. What resists automation is the evaluative and leadership piece — judging whether a suggested tool actually serves a specific group of K-12 learners, and coaching peers through adoption, both of which require in-person presence and professional judgment. The educator-preparation curriculum's technology-competency expectations persist across a catalog cycle, capping the erosion rather than eliminating the course's rationale. The instrumental case shifts from building multimedia artifacts by hand toward critically selecting, adapting, and modeling AI-assisted tools for colleagues and students, which is a real but partial erosion — landing the rating at Medium.

A decade out, AI-generated multimedia and adaptive learning environments will likely be standard tools in K-12 classrooms, and the course's original emphasis on building such artifacts personally has substantially eroded. What plausibly remains necessary is the human capacity to lead: evaluating whether an AI-recommended integration serves equity and learning goals, modeling responsible use around copyright and cyberbullying concerns, and coaching a school community through adoption — a role more about professional judgment and presence than production. Colorado's licensure framework, evolving slowly relative to model capability, continues in the central case to expect technology-integration competency somewhere in the educator-preparation curriculum. The genuine uncertainty is whether this becomes a leadership-and-evaluation course rather than a build-it-yourself course, not whether some version of the competency remains required for teacher candidates. Rating holds Medium, anchored by the partial institutional tether and the persistent in-person leadership component.
EDT 3010.d: This course is designed to give prospective teachers an overview of the advancement of technology in this digital age and its impacts on K-12 education. Students will explore emerging educational technologies and survey guidelines for selecting, managing, and evaluating technology tools to enhance teaching and learning. In addition to gaining skills in making multimedia projects, creating a web-based learning environment and using interactive technologies such as interactive whiteboard, students will also learn about issues such as copyrights, e-plagiarism, cyber-bullying, and security, etc. Students who finish this course successfully will become leaders in disseminating innovative ways of integrating technology in schools and through personal learning networks (PLNs).

r: This course applies knowledge of child development to instructional lesson plans that incorporate technologies shown to increase engagement in early-childhood classrooms, with interactive-board use integrated throughout, and it is co-requisite with an early-childhood-education course, embedding it inside that program's sequence. Lesson-plan drafting is meaningfully AI-exposed, but judging developmental appropriateness for very young children — screen time, attention, social-emotional impact — is precisely the kind of low-exposure, judgment-laden reasoning that requires domain expertise a model lacks direct access to, and the coreq linkage ties the course to a licensure-adjacent early-childhood curriculum a state framework helps shape. Errors here have real consequences for developing children, giving verification genuine weight even though it is not the dominant protective factor. At 24 months, AI assists drafting a lesson artifact, but the instrumental need for a candidate to develop this developmentally-grounded judgment is intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI lesson-generation tools tuned to early-childhood standards will likely be common, and much of the mechanical work of drafting technology-integrated lesson plans will be AI-assisted by default. But applying child-development knowledge to judge whether a given technology use is appropriate for a specific age group and classroom remains a verification task with real developmental stakes, and the jagged-frontier evidence suggests educators who defer to AI suggestions outside their actual competence — for instance, screen-heavy activities poorly matched to attention spans — risk worse outcomes than the tool implies. The coreq tie to the early-childhood-education sequence keeps this course inside a curriculum shaped by state expectations for teacher preparation, capping rather than removing the shift. The instrumental case moves toward evaluating and adapting AI-suggested technology use for developmental fit rather than producing lesson plans unaided, landing the rating at Medium.

Over ten years, AI-personalized early-childhood learning tools will likely be widespread, and the base task of matching a technology to a lesson goal becomes close to fully automatable. What remains is the harder judgment call: whether personalized AI tools serve a young child's actual developmental needs, an assessment that draws on child-development coursework this program pairs directly with technology methods. That judgment is exactly the non-obvious-failure territory task-exposure and jagged-frontier findings flag as durable, since a technology choice that looks pedagogically sound can still misserve a particular child's stage of development. Colorado's early-childhood teacher-preparation expectations persist in the central case, sustaining the coreq structure that embeds this course in the licensure pathway. The uncertainty is over how much of the lesson-building task fully automates versus how much developmental-fit judgment the course retains as its focus, not over whether some version of the course remains necessary. Rating holds Medium.
EDT 3020.d: An overview of the appropriate use and application of educational technology in a digital-aged early childhood classroom is provided. Students will learn the theories, skills, strategies, and tools that support the use of educational technology to facilitate effective teaching, learning, and assessment. Students will apply knowledge of child development and developmentally effective practice to develop instructional lesson plans that incorporate various types of technologies that have been shown to increase student engagement and learning. Effective use of interactive boards will be integrated throughout the course.

r: Students learn visual-design theory and perception principles to interpret existing instructional visuals and to select and develop their own, including digital-accessibility considerations, applying theories of visual processing to enhance learning and communication. Generating and interpreting visual design artifacts is squarely inside the reach of current generative image and design tools, and real-deliverable benchmarks already show top models approaching, though not yet matching, expert-level performance on comparable creative-production tasks. No licensure or accreditation body ties this specific course to a mandate, and its prerequisite (EDT 2050) gives it only a moderate foundational role within the design sequence, so the binding constraint is the design-exposure of the work itself. At 24 months, AI drafts visual concepts and even accessibility-compliant alternatives competently, but a human still needs to judge fit for a specific learning context and audience, which keeps this at Medium rather than High.

By 2031, AI image and design systems will generate polished, accessibility-aware instructional visuals rapidly, and productivity studies of AI-assisted creative and writing work already show large speed gains alongside quality that raters judge at least comparable — evidence extending naturally to visual-design production. The interpretive skill this course teaches, reading how a visual's structure and perceptual cues shape learning, becomes more valuable as an evaluation lens applied to AI-generated visuals than as a from-scratch production skill, but that shift itself represents real erosion of the course's original instrumental rationale. With no accreditation floor and only moderate scaffolding weight, nothing structurally holds the rating down. The rating rises to High, with the caveat that visual accessibility compliance retains a nontrivial verification component — a plausible-looking but non-compliant visual is a real failure mode — that keeps this from being treated as fully solved.

A decade out, AI visual and multimedia generation should be a routine, largely trusted part of instructional-design workflows, and the manual-production rationale for this course is substantially eroded in the central case, even as adoption across smaller institutions and school districts likely lags what capability alone would predict. What plausibly endures is directing and auditing that production: specifying learning-appropriate visual strategies, catching perceptual or accessibility failures an automated system misses, and adapting visuals to particular audiences and cultural contexts AI training data underrepresents. No licensure gate protects or restricts the course either way, so the rating tracks task-exposure directly rather than an institutional floor. The rating holds High under real uncertainty about how the instructional-design profession restructures around AI visual tools, and about how much of this course's content shifts from production technique to critical evaluation and creative direction.
EDT 3040.d: Students in this course explore the theories and principles of design of instructional visuals in the educational and professional settings. Students learn how to read and interpret meanings of existing instructional visuals by applying visual design theories and principles, and further to select and develop their own instructional visuals to enhance learning and communication. This course also includes basic theories of visual processing, perception, digital accessibility, and learning, which provides a foundation for interpreting, selecting, and developing effective instructional visuals.

r: The course teaches procedures for conceptualizing, designing, and incorporating game-based applications into instructional design across formal and informal settings, covering game-based theory, trends, and the foundational design and development skills needed to deploy such applications. Game-mechanics design and application prototyping are digital, highly AI-exposed activities — observed-usage data places computer-and-design work at the center of current AI deployment — and generative tools already produce game concepts, mechanics documents, and even playable prototypes competently. No licensure or accreditation mandate touches this course, and it functions as an applied elective with only moderate ties to the design sequence, so its rating rests on design-exposure rather than an institutional floor. At 24 months, a student still needs to judge which game mechanics actually serve a given instructional goal and audience, a strategic layer AI assists but does not fully replace, holding the rating at Medium.

By 2031, AI game- and application-design tools will generate playable instructional prototypes rapidly from a brief description of learning goals, and diffusion of generative design tools into edtech production pipelines will be considerably further along than today, even if overall firm-level AI adoption remains uneven. The distinctive human contribution shrinks toward specifying learning objectives and evaluating whether a generated game mechanic genuinely produces the intended instructional interaction rather than superficial engagement, a real narrowing of the course's original build-it-yourself scope. With no accreditation floor and only moderate foundational weight in the curriculum, nothing structurally caps the rating's rise. The rating moves to High, tempered by the honest recognition that judging whether gameplay actually teaches — as opposed to merely entertains — is a domain where plausible-looking AI output can mislead, so some verification value persists even as production itself becomes largely automated.

A decade out, generating full instructional games and interactive applications from a design brief should be routine for AI in the central case, substantially eroding the hands-on production rationale this course was built around. The residual human task is directing that production toward genuine learning outcomes and catching cases where an engaging game mechanic fails to teach the intended content, a judgment call that stays valuable precisely because it is easy for an automated system to optimize for engagement over instructional soundness. No licensure or accreditation lock protects or constrains the course at this horizon, so the rating continues to track the underlying task-exposure trend. The rating holds High, with wide uncertainty about how instructional game design as a discipline reorganizes once production is largely automated — plausibly toward a course centered entirely on instructional-interaction evaluation and creative direction rather than technical build skills.
EDT 3050.d: This course explores effective and structured procedures for conceptualizing, designing and incorporating game- based applications into the process of instructional design across formal and informal environments. Students will learn about game- based theory and trends, and acquire the foundational design and development skills necessary for deploying applications in a range of professional and educational settings.

r: This course applies multimedia-learning theory to design and develop digital instruction, working through principles of multimedia learning, typography, graphic design, audio and video production, and design processes toward real-world applications. Nearly every deliverable named here — typography choices, graphics, audio and video editing, multimedia storyboards — is a task type current generative and editing AI tools already perform at a competent level, and observed-usage data confirms computer-and-design work sits at the center of actual AI deployment today. No licensure or accreditation body constrains this course, and it draws on but is not itself a hard prerequisite for other courses in this batch, leaving design-exposure as the operative constraint. At 24 months, AI accelerates production of individual multimedia assets substantially, but a human still integrates them against multimedia-learning-theory principles like cognitive load and coherence, keeping the rating at Medium rather than High.

By 2031, AI multimedia systems will draft entire storyboards, generate graphics and video, and mix audio to a specified pedagogical brief with substantial fluency, and productivity research on AI-assisted creative and writing work already documents large time savings with output judged comparable or better — a pattern that plausibly extends across the full multimedia pipeline this course teaches. The remaining human contribution narrows to applying multimedia-learning-theory principles to specify and evaluate that output, rather than producing each asset by hand, a genuine erosion of the course's original scope. No accreditation lock or heavy foundational role protects the course from that shift. The rating rises to High, with appropriate hedging: multimedia-learning theory (managing cognitive load, avoiding split attention) is a real design-judgment skill, and AI systems optimized for visual appeal rather than learning outcomes can produce plausible but pedagogically unsound multimedia, keeping some evaluative burden human.

A decade out, producing polished instructional multimedia end to end will very plausibly be a routine AI capability, and the course's original hand-production rationale is substantially eroded in the central case, even as school and higher-ed adoption of the most advanced tools likely trails what raw capability would allow. What endures is the specification and evaluation layer: applying multimedia-learning principles to brief an AI system correctly and to judge whether its output actually reduces cognitive load and supports learning rather than merely looking polished. No licensure or accreditation floor governs this course either way, so the rating tracks the underlying automatability trend directly. The rating holds High, with real uncertainty about how instructional-multimedia work reorganizes once most production is automated — the most plausible shift is toward a course built entirely around multimedia-learning-theory application and critical evaluation of AI-generated instructional media.
EDT 3060.d: This course guides students through the process of applying design principles and multimedia learning theories to the design and development of effective digital multimedia instruction. Through the context of real world application, students explore principles of multimedia learning, design processes, typography, graphic design, audio and video production, as well as theoretical foundations, and multimedia design processes.

r: Teacher candidates in this course decide how technology supports P-12 content standards, learning, and assessment, then select, operate, and use media, computing, internet, and interactive-whiteboard tools to serve diverse learners' communication, professional-development, and productivity needs. The decision layer — matching a technology decision to specific standards and diverse student needs — is judgment work embedded in a live classroom context, distinct from the more AI-exposed task of operating a given tool. This course sits inside teacher-candidate preparation, where Colorado's educator-preparation framework expects technology-integration competency to be demonstrated, functioning as a partial but real institutional tether even though no clinical hours attach to it specifically. AI already assists drafting technology-integration plans, but at 24 months the instrumental need for a candidate to personally exercise this standards-and-equity judgment inside an accredited program is not materially eroded. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI tools will routinely draft technology-integration plans aligned to standards and assessment goals, and observed-usage data continues to show computer-and-office tasks as the largest actual-use category, meaning teacher candidates will be evaluating AI-suggested plans as a normal part of coursework. The jagged-frontier evidence matters directly: a candidate who accepts an AI-recommended tool without checking whether it actually serves a specific standard or a diverse learner's needs risks measurably worse decisions than the tool's confident presentation implies, sustaining a real verification role. The educator-preparation framework's technology-competency expectations persist across a catalog cycle, capping rather than eliminating the erosion. The instrumental case shifts from independently building integration plans toward critically evaluating and adapting AI-generated ones for standards alignment and equity, a genuine but partial narrowing of the original task, landing the rating at Medium.

A decade out, matching technology to standards and assessment goals will likely be substantially automatable, with AI systems drafting integration decisions that look competent by default. What plausibly remains necessary is the human check against equity and developmental appropriateness for actual diverse learners in a specific classroom, and the coordination of technology use across a classroom's real constraints — connectivity, access, student needs — that an AI planning tool cannot itself execute. Colorado's educator-preparation expectations for technology-integration competency, evolving slowly relative to model capability, likely persist in the central case, keeping a partial institutional tether in place. The genuine uncertainty is whether this becomes a course centered on auditing and coordinating AI-generated technology plans rather than building them from scratch, not whether some version of the standards-and-equity judgment remains required of teacher candidates. Rating holds Medium, anchored by that persistent judgment layer and the partial institutional tie.
EDT 3610.d: This course is designed to prepare teacher candidates to make decisions regarding the role of technology in support of content standards, learning, and assessment in P-12 education. Teacher candidates select, operate, and use media, computing, Internet, electronic interactive whiteboard, and related technologies to facilitate teaching/learning, communication, professional development, and productivity to meet the educational needs of diverse groups of learners.

r: This one-credit course trains teacher candidates to operate SMART Board and Promethean hardware and to translate that operational fluency into interactive K-12 lesson activities and assessments. The applied tasks, designing interactive slides, building formative-assessment activities, and adapting content to specific whiteboard software, map onto interacting-with-computers and documenting/recording-information work activities that generative tools already handle competently: drafting interactive quiz items, activity sequences, and lesson templates sits squarely inside current AI capability. Observed-usage data confirms computer-and-office tasks form the largest category of actual AI deployment today, and this course's content-authoring core sits there. No licensure clock-hours or foundational-scaffolding role protects it. At 24 months, general-purpose content-generation tools already replicate much of what students practice, though classroom deployment and hardware familiarity keep some hands-on residue, yielding a Medium rating rather than something higher.

By 2031, AI authoring tools will likely generate whiteboard-ready interactive activities, adaptive quizzes, and lesson sequences with minimal teacher input, further eroding the rationale for a stand-alone course on operating specific hardware and building its content by hand. Task-exposure research classifies content-generation and document-preparation work as strongly exposed, and this course's central task, producing interactive instructional materials for a named platform, sits inside that category rather than in the protected critical-reasoning band. Verification burden is modest: a flawed interactive activity is inspected and corrected easily by a classroom teacher, not a high-stakes failure. No credit-hour mandate or foundational-scaffolding role holds the rating down. The instrumental case for dedicating course time to manual whiteboard-content creation weakens substantially as authoring automates, pushing the rating to High even as genuine uncertainty remains about how quickly K-12 hardware itself evolves.

A decade out, interactive-whiteboard hardware may itself be displaced by more adaptive classroom AI systems, but the underlying instrumental question, whether a teacher candidate still needs dedicated instruction in manually building interactive lesson content for a named platform, points further toward automation. Capability-trend evidence indicates AI systems handle increasingly long, multi-step content-creation tasks, and diffusion into K-12 classroom-support tools is plausible by 2036 even though overall institutional AI adoption remains uneven today. No institutional lock-in or foundational role protects this narrow technology-skills course from that trajectory. The central-case rating is High, with the caveat that the specific hardware platforms named in the course may themselves be obsolete by then, a different but related form of erosion than pure task automation, and confidence at this horizon is accordingly lower.
EDT 3620.d: This course is designed to equip teacher candidates with knowledge and skills of interactive whiteboards in order to create effective and interactive lessons and activities that enhance teaching and learning in the K-12 classrooms, as well as to meet the need of most K-12 schools. Students will learn the basics and applications of interactive whiteboards, including SMART Board and Promethean Board commonly used in K-12 schools. Students will also apply the knowledge and skills of interactive whiteboards to creating interactive lessons, activities, and assessments.

r: Students in this course write competitive grant proposals against an actual request for proposal: a persuasive needs analysis, implementation plan, budget, and formative/summative evaluation design, culminating in a real submission to a funding source. Proposal narrative and budget-drafting are writing and business-documentation tasks; professional-writing productivity research finds large time savings and quality gains from AI assistance on exactly this kind of persuasive, structured document, and task-exposure research ranks writing among the most-exposed occupational activities. The course carries no licensure or accreditation lock and is not prerequisite substrate for later required coursework, so no protective cap applies. At 24 months, AI tools can already draft strong narrative and budget sections, though synthesizing a coherent, funder-specific strategy from a needs analysis still leans on human judgment, holding the rating to Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, AI systems will plausibly draft complete grant narratives, needs analyses, and budget justifications tailored to a funder's stated priorities with limited human editing, directly displacing the core deliverable this course teaches students to produce by hand. The professional-writing evidence base, showing substantial time reduction and quality improvement from AI-assisted drafting, applies almost directly to persuasive proposal writing, and verification burden here is moderate rather than severe: a weak proposal is rejected, not dangerous. No institutional mandate or foundational role caps the erosion. The instrumental case shifts toward strategic framing, funder-relationship judgment, and evaluating AI-drafted budgets for internal consistency rather than composing prose from scratch, real residual value, but not enough to prevent the rating from moving to High as the manual-drafting rationale weakens substantially.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems producing funder-ready grant narratives and budgets on demand, competent at tailoring tone and structure to a specific RFP, the exact skill set this course currently builds through supervised practice. Writing remains one of the task categories evidence most consistently places in the highly-exposed band, and nothing about grant-proposal composition sits outside that pattern. Without licensure gating or a scaffolding role protecting it, the course's instrumental rationale for teaching manual proposal drafting is substantially weakened by 2036 in the central case. The genuine uncertainty is whether the residual human value, funder-relationship strategy and verifying AI-generated budgets against institutional priorities, is enough to sustain a full course, or whether it becomes a briefer module inside broader coursework, which tempers confidence at this horizon.
EDT 3850.d: In this course, students will work collaboratively to write funding proposals for a current request for proposal (RFP). Participants will learn how to write a persuasive narrative, supported by a strong needs analysis, plan for implementation, budget, and evaluation. Special attention will be given to formative and summative evaluations, focusing on evaluation of implementation as well as impact of the proposed project. At the end of the semester, students will submit their proposals to funding sources.

r: The course trains students to apply advanced instructional-design models and learning theories to build inclusive, complex learning environments, integrating adaptive-learning systems and emerging technology through hands-on projects. Producing instructional content, activity sequences, and assessment design maps onto interacting-with-computers and developing-objectives-and-strategies work activities that generative AI tools already perform at a real, if imperfect, level; GDPval-style evaluation of AI on real occupational deliverables finds current models approaching but still below expert parity on this kind of integrated design work. The course is not licensure-gated and is not tightly load-bearing for later required coursework, so no protective cap holds the rating down. At 24 months AI assists drafting and prototyping, but inclusive-design judgment for diverse learners still requires meaningful instructor-guided practice, keeping the rating at Medium.

By 2031, AI-assisted authoring and adaptive-learning-system design tools will plausibly generate substantial portions of an instructional design, objectives, activity sequences, assessments, even accessibility accommodations, challenging the rationale for manually practicing full-cycle design. The jagged-frontier research is directly relevant: AI performs well on well-specified design sub-tasks but produces less reliable results on judgment calls about a specific learner population's needs, and users miscalibrated toward AI output are measurably less accurate outside the tool's strong suit. Verification burden is moderate, not severe, and no institutional lock-in or strong scaffolding role protects the course. The instrumental case shifts toward critically evaluating and adapting AI-generated designs for inclusivity and context rather than authoring from a blank page, a real shift but not enough to hold the rating below High.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems producing full draft instructional designs, including adaptive-learning configurations, from a stated set of learning objectives and audience constraints, substantially eroding the case for hands-on manual design practice as this course currently structures it. Capability-trend evidence indicates the length and complexity of tasks AI can reliably complete is growing quickly, and instructional design's largely digital, project-based work sits well within that trajectory. No licensure or foundational-scaffolding protection applies. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the designer's value migrates to specifying constraints, auditing AI output for equity and accessibility, and iterating with stakeholders rather than direct authorship, meaningful residual work, but the instrumental case for a course centered on manual design production is substantially weakened by 2036 in the central case.
EDT 4010.d: Students in this course delve into sophisticated methodologies and strategies for crafting effective instructional materials and experiences. Students apply advanced instructional design models and learning theories, with a focus on integrating emerging technologies and adaptive learning systems. Through hands-on projects, students gain expertise in designing complex learning environments that inclusively meet the needs of diverse learners and contexts. The course emphasizes critical analysis, iterative design processes, and the application of best practices in creating impactful educational interventions.

r: Students learn to plan, schedule, and budget instructional-design projects and to apply the human-performance-technology framework: diagnosing performance gaps, designing targeted interventions, and measuring intervention effectiveness against organizational goals. Scheduling, budgeting, and progress-tracking are core project-management activities that observed-usage data places inside the largest actual category of current AI deployment, computer-and-office work, and enterprise API usage already skews heavily toward automation rather than augmentation on exactly this kind of structured task. Diagnosing a genuine organizational performance problem still requires context the AI does not have, so verification stays meaningful. No licensure lock or heavy scaffolding role protects the course. At 24 months, project-tracking and reporting tasks are already substantially automatable, while diagnostic and stakeholder-alignment work retains enough human judgment to keep the rating at Medium.

By 2031, AI project-management assistants will plausibly handle scheduling, budget tracking, milestone reporting, and even first-draft performance-gap diagnoses with limited human intervention, directly displacing much of what this course teaches students to do manually. Enterprise usage data already shows automation dominating augmentation on structured business-process tasks at a high rate, and diffusion into ed-tech and corporate-training project workflows is a plausible extension by this horizon even though overall firm-level AI adoption remains uneven today. Verification burden is moderate, a misdiagnosed performance problem wastes resources but is not catastrophic, and no institutional mandate protects the course. The instrumental case shifts toward directing AI-run project workflows and validating its performance-gap diagnoses against organizational context, a real but narrower competence, pushing the rating to High.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems autonomously managing routine project schedules, budgets, and status reporting, and generating credible first-pass human-performance-technology interventions from stated organizational symptoms, precisely the tasks this course builds. Compute and capability trends suggest multi-step, longer-horizon project coordination is within reach for AI systems by 2036, and nothing about instructional-design project management sits outside the exposed, digitally-native task categories the evidence base repeatedly identifies. No licensure gate or deep scaffolding role holds the rating down. The honest uncertainty is how much organizational-diagnosis judgment remains irreducibly human as AI absorbs the administrative and analytical layers of project management; the central case still finds the course's manual-execution rationale substantially eroded, supporting a High rating with real but bounded confidence at this horizon.
EDT 4020.d: Students in this course are provided a comprehensive overview of project management principles and human performance technology (HPT) as they apply to instructional design. Students learn how to manage and execute instructional design projects effectively, including planning, scheduling, budgeting, and evaluating project outcomes. The course also includes the HPT framework, focusing on diagnosing performance issues, designing targeted interventions, and measuring the effectiveness of instructional solutions. By the end of the course, students are equipped with the skills to lead projects, align instructional strategies with organizational goals, and drive performance improvements.

r: This course has students review published instructional-design research and job descriptions, then debate findings with practicing designers to synthesize current trends, applying one or more theories to real-world projects in order to critically re-imagine the field. The core work is interpretive and dialogic, evaluating competing claims about the field's direction and defending a position to practitioners in live discussion, which task-exposure research consistently finds negatively associated with AI exposure, unlike routine content generation. The interpersonal debate component adds a real-time, less digitally-fungible element. No licensure lock or foundational-scaffolding role is at play. At 24 months, AI can summarize trend literature, but the course's actual graded work, critical synthesis and live professional debate, remains only lightly touched, holding the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI research-synthesis tools will more capably summarize instructional-design literature and generate plausible trend narratives, narrowing the informational gap this course closes through independent reading. But the graded work is critical evaluation and live debate with practicing designers, not synthesis alone, and critical-thinking-intensive tasks remain the category evidence most reliably places outside AI's comparative advantage. Verification burden is moderate: a shallow trend analysis is caught by an instructor or practitioner in discussion, not silently accepted. No institutional mandate protects or restricts the course structurally. The instrumental case erodes somewhat as literature synthesis automates, but the interpretive and dialogic core persists, moving the rating to Medium, real erosion in the preparatory work, limited erosion in the course's central competence at this horizon.

Over a decade, capability trends suggest AI systems will engage in increasingly sophisticated, multi-turn argumentation about professional trends, potentially serving as a genuine interlocutor rather than just a summarizer, a meaningfully different and more exposed position than today's simple retrieval-and-summary tools. If AI can competently debate emerging instructional-design issues and generate innovative theoretical applications, the instrumental rationale for a course built around human debate with practitioners weakens substantially. This is a wide-uncertainty prediction: it depends on how much professional discourse itself becomes AI-mediated by 2036, far less established than capability growth in content generation. No structural protection applies. The central case moves the rating to High, held with meaningfully lower confidence than the nearer-term horizons given how much rests on speculative diffusion into professional discourse practices.
EDT 4050.d: This course examines current trends and issues relating to the everyday practice of instructional design, including the application of universal design. Students are provided opportunities to review published instructional design research, thought leadership, and job descriptions in K-12, Higher Education, and corporate settings, as well as debate findings with practicing instructional designers in order to understand key trends in the field. This course also guides students to examine instructional design best-practice and apply one or more theories/models to real-world instructional projects in an effort to innovatively evolve/redefine instructional design and/or the role of instructional designers.

r: The capstone requires students to independently plan, execute, and defend an original instructional-design project addressing multicultural, accessibility, and diversity considerations, integrating skills from across the program with limited instructor scaffolding. Because the course's explicit purpose is demonstrating the student's own independent synthesis and originality rather than producing a deliverable AI could substitute directly, its instrumental core sits closer to critical-thinking and judgment work than to routine content production, the category task-exposure research consistently finds least exposed. GDPval-style evaluation shows AI approaching but still below expert parity on integrated, real-world deliverables requiring this kind of end-to-end judgment. No licensure gate applies, and as a terminal capstone it scaffolds nothing later. At 24 months the course's demonstrated-independence purpose keeps the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI tools will more capably assist with individual components of a capstone project, drafting design documents, generating accessibility checklists, prototyping content, narrowing the amount of the deliverable a student must produce entirely unaided. But the course's instrumental purpose is verifying that the student personally can plan, execute, and defend original integrated work, a judgment- and originality-heavy task that remains harder to fully delegate, and GDPval-type evidence shows real gaps between AI and expert-level integrated deliverables persisting. Verification burden is moderate: a design that merely looks polished but lacks genuine synthesis is still detectable by faculty evaluators. No structural protection or cap changes at this horizon. The instrumental case erodes as component tasks automate, moving the rating to Medium while the demonstrated-originality core still resists full substitution.

A decade out, if AI systems can independently plan and execute complete, well-integrated instructional-design projects to a professional standard, the specific evidentiary function of a capstone, proving the student can do this unaided, becomes harder to distinguish from AI-assisted output, and the course's instrumental rationale weakens substantially in the central case. Capability trends toward longer, more autonomous task completion make this a plausible trajectory by 2036, though it remains a genuinely uncertain prediction about both AI capability and how assessment is redesigned in response. No licensure or scaffolding protection applies, and as a terminal course it carries no downstream dependency. The rating moves to High, held with meaningfully lower confidence than the nearer horizons given how much depends on unresolved questions about capstone assessment design under ubiquitous AI.
EDT 4060.d: This capstone course is intended to provide students with the opportunity to develop and implement instructional design learning experiences and processes. As a fundamental component of the Capstone course, students will be responsible for completing a capstone project that demonstrates their understanding of the topic they select for their project with the multicultural, accessible, and diversity considerations as well as how the topic can be applied to real life practices. The capstone project also provides the opportunity for students to demonstrate independence and originality, to plan and organize a project over a period of time, and to put into practice some of the concepts and skills introduced in all other courses of the program.

r: This capstone field placement embeds students for 135 hours inside an actual instructional-design team or professional's workplace, assisting on live projects and building a reflective portfolio around the experience. The instrumental value here is not a discrete, AI-substitutable output but supervised professional practice, real-time collaboration, mentorship, and workplace judgment under a practicing designer's direct oversight. Task-exposure research finds AI usage concentrated in computer-and-office content tasks, not in the interpersonal mentorship and situated organizational learning this placement is built around, and verifying that a student has genuinely developed professional competency requires a human supervisor's direct assessment, not an AI proxy. There is a structured, fixed-hours field requirement functioning much like a practicum. At 24 months the placement's embodied, mentored, in-workplace core is essentially untouched by current AI capability.

By 2031, AI tools will handle more of the routine content-production tasks a student might be asked to assist with on placement, but the course's instrumental purpose, supervised entry into real professional practice, relationship-building, and workplace acculturation, is not a task AI performs on the student's behalf. The jagged-frontier evidence is relevant in reverse here: novices benefit most from human mentorship precisely because they lack the judgment to know when AI-assisted work is wrong, which is exactly what a workplace placement teaches through direct supervision. Diffusion of AI into workplaces is real but still uneven at the firm level. The fixed clock-hour structure keeps the placement requirement in place across a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low; AI changes what interns help produce, not whether supervised professional immersion remains necessary.

A decade out, even if AI performs most of the routine design tasks an intern might otherwise assist with, the placement's core instrumental function, a novice practitioner learning professional judgment, workplace norms, and how to work alongside experienced designers and their tools under real accountability, is not the kind of task that gets automated away; if anything, learning to supervise and validate AI-assisted design work is best learned in a live professional setting with a mentor present. The uncertainty is genuine about how thoroughly AI reshapes the day-to-day content of instructional-design work by 2036, but that uncertainty concerns what interns do, not whether structured, mentored field experience remains instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low, anchored by the embodied, supervised nature of the placement itself.
EDT 4090.d: This capstone course is intended to provide students with exposure to a professional work setting related to instructional design. Students will complete 135 hours working in the field of instructional design. Students will assist a professional instructional designer or design team in order to gain insight and experience. Students will also reflect on their experience and demonstrate their learning outcome through a portfolio.
